en: The Perfection of Wisdom in Twenty-Five Thousand Lines (Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā).
Homage to the Omniscient One!

Thus have I heard: at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagṛha on Vulture Peak Mountain together with a great saṅgha of about five thousand monks, all of whom were arhats— whose taints were exhausted,

who were free from afflictions, who had attained mastery, whose minds were well-liberated, whose wisdom was well-liberated, who were noble steeds, great elephants, and who had accomplished what was to be done.

Together with five hundred bhikṣuṇīs who had accomplished what was to be done, laid down their burdens, attained their own goal, exhausted the fetters of existence, whose minds were well-liberated through perfect knowledge, and who had reached the supreme perfection of mastery over all states of mind; and together with many hundreds of thousands of nayutas of koṭis of bodhisattvas, all of whom had seen the Dharma in this very life.

All of them had attained the *dhāraṇīs*, dwelt in emptiness, had the signless as their sphere of activity, were free from conceptualization regarding their vows, had attained the equality of patience, had attained the unattached *dhāraṇīs*, possessed infallible superknowledges, and their words were authoritative. They were without guile or deceit, free from thoughts of gain or fame, taught the Dharma without worldly motive, and had reached the further shore of patience regarding the profound Dharma.

They had attained fearlessness, had completely transcended the works of Māra, had laid to rest the obscurations of karma, were skilled in the analytical discernment and exposition of the Dharma, and had well undertaken their vows for incalculable eons. They possessed smiling faces, were the first to speak, and were free from frowning countenances;
they were skilled in conversing with verses and songs, were devoid of a dejected mind, possessed uninterrupted eloquence, and were endowed with the confidence that overcomes infinite assemblies.

They were skilled in emerging from infinite millions of eons; they had resolute faith in dharmas that are like an illusion, a mirage, the moon reflected in water, a dream, an echo, an optical illusion, a reflection, and a magical creation; they were skilled in entering the subtle and manifold inclinations regarding the conduct of beings in their various realms of existence; they possessed unimpeded minds and were endowed with supreme patience;
they were skilled in entering into the nature of reality as it is; and they were sustained by the setting forth of vows for the infinite arrays of all buddha-fields.

They were constantly and continuously present before them through the samādhi of recollecting the Buddhas of incalculable world-systems; they were skilled in supplicating immeasurable Buddhas, skilled in pacifying various views, latent tendencies, outbursts, and afflictions, and skilled in accomplishing hundreds of thousands of playful manifestations of samādhi.
Namely: the bodhisattva mahāsattva Badhrapāla, Ratnākara, Susārthavāha,
Naradatta, Varuṇadatta, Guhagupta, Indradatta, Uttaramati, Viśeṣamati,
Vardhamānamati, Amoghadarśin, Susaṃprasthita, and Suvikrāntavikrāmin.

And with the Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas Nityodyukta, Nityaprayukta, Anikṣiptadhura, Sūryagarbha, Anupamamati, Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, Mañjuśrī, Vajramati, Ratnamudrāhasta, Nityotkṣiptahasta, and Maitreya.
With these as their leaders, there were many hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kotis of bodhisattvas.
Then the Blessed One himself prepared a lion-throne and sat down, folding his legs crosswise and setting his body erect;
all the [unfavorable] moments ceased, and those beings who had passed away from those states of hell,
the animal realm, and the world of Yama were all reborn among gods and humans, having been reborn among gods and humans through the very power of the Blessed One.
They recollected their former births; having recollected them, with that very joy and gladness, they approached the presence of those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, in their respective Buddha-fields.
Having approached and performed prostrations at the feet of those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, they all stood with palms joined and paid homage to those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones.

Then, indeed, at that very instant, moment, and second, those beings who were blind in this triple-thousand great-thousandfold world system saw forms with their eyes; those who were deaf heard sounds with their ears;
those who were insane regained their mindfulness; those with distracted minds became one-pointed in mind; and those who were naked [were clothed].

Those who were clothed in robes became hungry; those whose limbs were full became thirsty; those who were free from thirst became afflicted by disease; those who were afflicted by disease became free from disease; those with impaired faculties became possessed of complete faculties;

and those beings who had not desisted from unwholesome conduct of body, speech, and mind, and from wrong livelihood, became those who had desisted from unwholesome conduct of body, speech, and mind, and from wrong livelihood.
All sentient beings came to possess minds equal toward their mothers and fathers; they possessed minds equal toward brothers and sisters;

they possessed minds equal toward friends, ministers, kinsmen, and blood relations. They became practitioners of the ten paths of wholesome action, celibate, pure, free from the stench of raw flesh, and endowed with all happiness; they attained such happiness as follows: just as if...
At that very time, those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones residing in other Buddha-fields, came to be endowed with such wisdom that they uttered this inspired utterance:
"Excellent is self-control! Excellent is tranquility! Excellent is restraint! Excellent is the life lived in the holy life! Excellent is non-violence toward living beings!"
Then, indeed, the Blessed One, seated upon that very lion-throne, remained surpassing this great trichiliocosm world-system;
he shone, glowed, heated, and radiated with splendor, color, majesty, and brilliance,
[illuminating] worlds as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges in the eastern direction, the southern, the western, the northern, below, above, and in the intermediate directions.
Having overcome all, the Tathāgata stands, shines, blazes, and radiates with splendor, complexion, majesty, and brilliance.

Just as Sumeru, the king of mountains, stands surpassing all other mountains, shining, glowing, blazing, and radiating with splendor, color, glory, and brilliance, even so the Blessed One stood surpassing all world-systems, shining, glowing, blazing, and radiating with splendor, color, glory, and brilliance.
Then the Blessed One once again manifested an ordinary physical body identical to the physical bodies of the sentient beings within the triple-thousand great-thousandfold world system.

Then, indeed, as many gods as there were in this triple-thousand great-thousand world-system— those belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa heaven, the Brahmakāyika gods, the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods, the Nirmāṇarati gods, the Tuṣita gods, and the Yāma gods— [all gathered].

And the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven and the Cāturmahārājakāyika heaven, having seen that unspeakably beautiful body of the Tathāgata, took divine flowers; they took divine perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, and flags;
and they took divine blue lotuses, white water lilies, fragrant lilies, white lotuses, and red lotuses, as well as divine keśara and tamāla leaves.

Having taken them, they approached that Tathāgata’s unsurpassed physical form; and those humans who were here in this triple-thousand great-thousandfold world system, having seen that unsurpassed physical form of the Tathāgata, also took flowers growing on land and in water and approached that Tathāgata’s unsurpassed physical form.

Then indeed those gods and those humans scattered, showered, and strewn that body of the Tathāgata with those divine flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, and flags, as well as with flowers growing on land and in water.
Then, indeed, those showers of flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, and flags,

as well as the terrestrial and aquatic flowers with which the Blessed One was strewn, all of them, through the Blessed One’s supernatural power, were established in the sky above as a single gabled pavilion equal in size to the triple-thousand great thousandfold world system.
And from that gabled pavilion, divine flower garlands and silk streamers hung down, dangled, and were suspended;
and by those flower garlands and silk streamers, this great trichiliocosm world-system was exceedingly beautified,
as was the golden-colored radiance of the Blessed One’s majesty spread throughout the ten directions.
In each and every direction, world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges became filled and illuminated.

And in this great trichiliocosm, in every world-system of four continents, it occurred to each of the gods and humans: "The Tathāgata is seated before me, teaching the Dharma; he is seated before me."
"The Tathāgata is seated, teaching the Dharma."

Then, indeed, the Blessed One, seated upon that very lion-throne, again smiled; by the radiance of that smile, this trichiliocosm was suffused with light, and as far as world-systems in the ten directions equal in number to the sands of the river Gaṅgā were suffused with light— all those [beings] who were here in this trichiliocosm.

Those beings in the eastern direction saw the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, together with their assemblies of śrāvakas in world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā; and those beings who were in the world-systems in the eastern direction, as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, [beheld] this Sahā world-system.
They beheld the Tathāgata Śākyamuni together with the community of monks; likewise, in the southern direction,
in the western, northern, intermediate directions, and in the regions below and above— in world systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā—
they beheld the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, together with their assemblies of disciples, as well as all the sentient beings in those world systems.
They beheld this Sahā world-system and the Tathāgata Śākyamuni together with the community of monks.
Then, indeed, having passed beyond world-systems in the eastern direction as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, there is a world-system at the very end of them called Ratnāvatī.
There, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksambuddha named Ratnākara dwells, stays, and maintains himself; he teaches this very Perfection of Wisdom to the Bodhisattvas. Now, in that world-system...

The bodhisattva mahāsattva named Samantaraśmi, having seen that great radiance, that great earthquake, and having seen the Lord’s beautiful physical form, approached the place where the Blessed One Ratnākara,
the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksambuddha was; having approached, [he bowed at] the feet of that Blessed One.

Having paid homage to that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Ratnākara, he said this to him: "Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the condition, for the appearance in the world of this great radiance, of this great earthquake, and of the manifestation of the body of this most wonderful Tathāgata?"
When this had been said, the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Ratnākara, spoke thus to the Bodhisattva Samantaraśmi:

"Noble son, to the west of here, beyond world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, there is a world-system named Sahā. There dwells, remains, and sustains himself the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Śākyamuni."
He sustains himself and fully reveals the perfection of wisdom of the bodhisattvas; such is its power.
Then the bodhisattva Samantaraśmi said this to the Tathāgata Ratnākara:

"Blessed One, I shall go to that Sahā world-system to behold, pay homage to, and attend upon the Blessed One Śākyamuni, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksambuddha, as well as those bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas."

To show him those who were for the most part youths, who had attained the dhāraṇīs, who were skilled in the production of samādhis, and who had reached the further shore of mastery over all samādhis, the Blessed One said: "Go, noble son, whenever you deem it the right time."

Then the Tathāgata Ratnākara gave to the Bodhisattva Samantaraśmi lotuses made of various jewels, shining with gold and having a thousand petals, and spoke to him thus: "O son of good family, with these lotuses you and your retinue should scatter over that Tathāgata Śākyamuni, and you should say: 'The Blessed One Ratnākara...'"

He inquires after the Blessed One’s freedom from illness, freedom from affliction, ease of movement, well-being, strength, and comfortable dwelling; and he presents these thousand-petaled lotuses made of various jewels and shining with gold, which were sent by that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Ratnākara, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
"O son of good family, you must go with full awareness that these lotuses have been sent by the Blessed One to that buddha-field.
And why is that? Because, son of good family, those bodhisattvas who have been born there in this Sahā world-system are difficult to approach."

Then, indeed, the bodhisattva Samantaraśmi, having taken from that Tathāgata Ratnākara those lotuses made of various jewels— golden-hued and possessing a thousand petals— was surrounded and escorted by many hundreds of thousands of nayutas of koṭis of bodhisattvas,
both householders and renunciants, as well as boys and girls, and set out toward the eastern direction.
Honoring, revering, respecting, and worshiping those Blessed Buddhas— numbering as many as the sands of the river Ganges—
with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, flags, and victory-pennants,
he arrived in this Sahā world-system, where the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, the Arhat, the Samyaksambuddha, was staying.

He approached him; having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and stood to one side. Standing to one side, the bodhisattva Samantaraśmi said this to the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni:
"The Blessed One Ratnākara inquires after the Blessed One’s freedom from illness, freedom from affliction, and ease of movement."
He inquired after [the Blessed One’s] well-being, strength, and ease of movement, and the Blessed One Ratnākara,
the Tathāgata, sent these thousand-petaled lotuses made of various jewels and shining with gold as a gift for the Blessed One.

Then the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, took those lotuses and cast them toward those world systems in the eastern direction, as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges; by those lotuses, those world systems were completely filled, and within those lotuses, forms of Buddhas sat and taught the Dharma in those Buddha-fields.
They taught this very teaching connected with the perfection of wisdom; and all those beings who heard that Dharma became fixed in their destiny toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Then indeed, those bodhisattva mahāsattvas— both householders and renunciants, as well as boys and girls—
who had come from that world-system Ratnavatī together with the bodhisattva mahāsattva Samantaraśmi,
honored, revered, respected, and worshipped the Blessed One Śākyamuni by means of their respective roots of merit.

Having prostrated with their heads at his feet, they sat down to one side. Seated there, those householders, those renunciants, those boys, and those girls said this to the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni: "The Blessed One, the Tathāgata Ratnākara, inquires after the Blessed One’s freedom from affliction, freedom from illness, and ease of movement."

He inquires after [the Blessed One’s] journey, strength, and well-being in his comfortable dwelling; and these lotuses have been sent to the Blessed One by that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Ratnākara. Then, indeed, the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, [took] those lotuses...

Śāriputra, it is precisely through such mental attention that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, accomplishes the gift of the realization of the superknowledge of recollecting former abodes. With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans,
he beholds beings passing away and being reborn— beautiful and ugly, lowly and exalted, in happy destinies and miserable destinies, according to their karma.
He understands beings as they truly are: "These worthy beings, being possessed of misconduct of body, possessed of misconduct of speech, and possessed of misconduct of mind;

revilers of the noble ones and holders of wrong views—because of their undertaking of actions based on wrong view, upon the breakup of the body after death, they are reborn in states of deprivation, in evil destinies, in perdition, in the hells. But these other worthy beings..."

With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, [he sees] beings who are endowed with good conduct of body, endowed with good conduct of speech and good conduct of mind, who do not revile the noble ones, and who hold right view; because of their undertaking of actions based on right view, after the breaking up of the body, after death, they are reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world.

He understands, as it truly is, the passing away and rebirth of beings belonging to the six realms of existence in all world-systems throughout the ten directions, as far as the limits of the realm of space; yet by means of that divine eye he does not conceive pride, for that eye is no-eye on account of its inconceivability. He does not conceive, "I am one who sees," nor does he perceive that very eye, because of its emptiness of intrinsic nature.

Based on the fact that intrinsic nature is devoid [of self-existence] and based on the fact that intrinsic nature is unarisen, he does not even produce the thought of the divine eye, nor the thought of the actualization of the divine eye, except for the mental engagement with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). For it is thus, Śāriputra, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom [attains] the knowledge of the realization of the superknowledge of the divine eye.

He brings forth the knowledge of the realization of the superknowledge of the destruction of the outflows; he does not fall into the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha, nor does he aspire to any other dharma whatsoever, except that he will fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. By virtue of his skill in bringing forth that knowledge of the superknowledge of the realization of the destruction of the outflows, he...

He does not conceive [the thought], "I know this," because that knowledge is non-knowledge by virtue of its inconceivability. He does not conceive, "I am he who knows," because he does not apprehend that very knowledge by virtue of its emptiness of intrinsic nature, its isolation from intrinsic nature, and the non-apprehension of intrinsic nature. He does not even arouse the volition for the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya-jñāna-cetanā*), nor the volition for the accomplishment of the superknowledge of the realization of the destruction of the outflows.

Except for the mental engagement with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in this way in the perfection of wisdom does not bring forth the superknowledge of the realization of the exhaustion of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*). Furthermore, Śāriputra, as a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in the perfection of wisdom, the six superknowledges are fulfilled and the superknowledges are purified.
Being completely purified, they enter into the knowledge of all modes.

There are, Śāriputra, bodhisattva mahāsattvas who, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, abide in the perfection of giving and purify the path to all-aspect omniscience by means of absolute emptiness,
on account of its being ungraspable.

There are, Śāriputra, bodhisattva mahāsattvas who, while practicing the perfection of wisdom and abiding in the perfection of ethical discipline, purify the path to all-aspect omniscience by means of absolute emptiness, on account of being beyond transgression.

There are, Śāriputra, bodhisattvas mahāsattvas who, practicing in the perfection of wisdom and abiding in the perfection of patience, purify the path to the knowledge of all aspects by means of absolute emptiness,
on account of its unshakeability.

There are, Śāriputra, bodhisattva mahāsattvas who, practicing in the perfection of wisdom and established in the perfection of vigor, purify the path to all-aspect omniscience by means of absolute emptiness, on account of the non-laxity of physical and mental vigor.

There are, Śāriputra, bodhisattvas mahāsattvas who, while practicing the perfection of wisdom and abiding in the perfection of meditative concentration, purify the path to the knowledge of all aspects by means of absolute emptiness,
based upon an undistracted mind.
“Śāriputra, there are bodhisattva mahāsattvas who, while practicing the perfection of wisdom,

purify the path to omniscience by means of abandoning the mind of faulty wisdom. Indeed, Śāriputra, it is in this way that bodhisattva mahāsattvas, established in the six perfections, purify the path to omniscience through absolute emptiness.”
Based on the state of neither coming nor going, and based on non-appropriation—for what reason is that [perfection] designated? Generosity is designated based on grasping;
ethical discipline based on immorality; patience based on impatience; vigor based on laziness;
meditative concentration based on lack of composure; and wisdom is designated based on faulty wisdom. That is how it is designated.

He does not think, "I have crossed over," nor does he think, "I have not crossed over. He does not think, "giving" or "miserliness"; he does not think, "virtue" or "immorality"; he does not think, "patience" or "agitation"; he does not think, "diligence" or "laziness"; he does not think, "concentration" or "lack of concentration"; he does not think, "wisdom" or "poor wisdom. He does not think, "I am a winner," nor does he think, "I am honored," nor does he think, "I am dishonored."

For what reason? Because, Śāriputra, non-arising does not think, "I have been drawn forth," nor does it think, "I have been saluted," "I have been honored," or "I have been dishonored. For what reason? Because, Śāriputra, while a bodhisattva mahāsattva courses here in the perfection of wisdom, the perfection of wisdom completely cuts off all conceits.
Those qualities which exist are not found among the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Fulfilling these qualities, he brings sentient beings to maturity, purifies the Buddha-fields, and attains the knowledge of all aspects.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he generates a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings; having generated a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings, he attains the equality of all phenomena;
and having attained that equality of all phenomena, [he establishes] all sentient beings within that equality of all phenomena.
He establishes [this] in the very present life; he becomes dear and pleasing to the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones,
and he becomes dear and pleasing to all bodhisattvas, all śrāvakas, and all pratyekabuddhas, wherever [he may be].

Wherever he is reborn, there he never sees unpleasant forms with his eyes, nor hears unpleasant sounds with his ears, nor smells unpleasant odors with his nose, nor tastes unpleasant flavors with his tongue,
nor touches unpleasant tangibles with his body, nor cognizes unpleasant mental phenomena with his mind; and he does not fall away from them.
Of the knowledge of all aspects.

Furthermore, while this teaching on the perfection of wisdom was being expounded, three hundred monks from that assembly covered the Blessed One with the robes they were wearing and generated the resolve for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Then the Blessed One indeed smiled.

Then the venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, and bowing with palms joined toward the Blessed One, addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"What, O Blessed One, is the cause, what is the condition for manifesting this smile? For Buddhas do not manifest a smile without cause or without condition."
The Blessed Ones manifest a smile.

The Blessed One said: "Ānanda, these three hundred monks, having passed away from here, will be reborn in the Buddha-field of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksambuddha Akṣobhya, in the world-system Abhirati. In the Tārakopama kalpa, during the sixty-first aeon, they will arise in the world as Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksambuddhas named Mahāketu."

And sixty thousand sons of gods in this assembly have been brought to maturity by this teaching of the Dharma; they shall attain final nirvana in the presence of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksambuddha Maitreya.

Then, at that time, by the power of the Blessed One Śākyamuni, the four assemblies from the circle of the Blessed One’s retinue beheld a thousand Buddhas in the eastern direction, together with the magnificent arrays of qualities of their great Buddha-fields;
likewise in the southern direction, the western, the northern, the northeastern, the southeastern, and the southwestern directions.
In the west-north, below and above, and in each of the [other] directions, they saw a thousand Buddhas,
each endowed with a magnificent array of qualities of a Buddha-field; yet they did not see such arrays of qualities of Buddha-fields here in this Sahā world-system as they saw in the ten directions.
Of those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones.
Then, indeed, ten thousand living beings from the circle of the assembly of the Blessed One Śākyamuni made these aspirations:
"O Blessed One, we shall perform those meritorious deeds by which merits we may be reborn in these Buddha-fields."
Then the Blessed One, having understood the intention of those sons of good family, at that moment smiled.
Ānanda said: "What, Blessed One, is the cause, what is the reason for manifesting this smile? For Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, do not manifest a smile without cause or without reason."
The Blessed One said, "Ānanda, do you see these ten thousand beings? Ānanda replied, "I see them, Blessed One.

The Blessed One said, "Ānanda, these ten thousand beings, having passed away from here, will be reborn in these Buddha-fields in the ten directions, and they shall never be separated from the Tathāgatas; after that, they will become Tathāgatas named Vyūharāja."
Arhats, perfectly awakened ones, will arise in the world.
Then indeed, the venerable Śāriputra,
the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the venerable Subhūti, the venerable Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra,
the venerable Mahākāśyapa, and these and many other well-known monks who were bodhisattvas—

And the great beings—the monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—said this to the Blessed One: "O Blessed One, this is a great perfection; this is a sublime perfection for the Bodhisattvas, the great beings, namely, the perfection of wisdom.
It is the foremost perfection, the distinguished perfection, the supreme perfection, the excellent perfection, the refined perfection, and the unsurpassed perfection."

This perfection, O Blessed One, is the unsurpassed perfection; it is the unequaled perfection; it is the perfection equal to the unequalled; it is the perfection of space; it is the perfection of the emptiness of intrinsic characteristics;

it is the perfection endowed with all virtues; it is the perfection endowed with all forms of emptiness; it is the invincible perfection—namely, the perfection of wisdom of the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas. For herein, O Blessed One, in this perfection of wisdom...

By those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who have practiced giving with the incomparable, the incomparable perfection of generosity has been fulfilled; by them, for the sake of attaining an incomparable physical existence, they will become possessors of the equal and peerless Dharma, namely, unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.
Thus, by them the incomparable morality, patience, vigor, and meditative concentration have been cultivated;

by them the incomparable perfection of wisdom has been fulfilled; by them an incomparable physical form has been attained; they shall become possessors of the equal-and-equal Dharma, namely, unsurpassed perfect enlightenment—and it is in this very Perfection of Wisdom, O Blessed One, that you [are established].

While practicing, he became an attainer of incomparable form; he became an attainer of incomparable feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; he fully awakened to incomparable enlightenment and set in motion the wheel of Dharma that is equal to the unequalled.
In this very same way, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the past, future, and present [attain] in this very Perfection of Wisdom.

Practicing for the sake of awakening to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they have awakened, they are awakening, and they will awaken; therefore, O Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to reach the further shore of all dharmas should apply themselves to the perfection of wisdom and should pay homage to those bodhisattva mahāsattvas, O Blessed One.
Those who practice this perfection of wisdom are [honored] by the world with its gods, humans, and asuras.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to those many great śrāvakas and those bodhisattva mahāsattvas:
"It is so, noble sons, it is so! Those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who course in this perfection of wisdom are to be honored by the world with its gods, humans, and asuras."
For what reason? It is because, O sons of good family, by depending upon the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, there is the manifestation in the world of the human realm,

as well as in the world of the gods, of the great kṣatriya clans, the great brahmin clans, the great householder clans, of the universal monarchs, and of the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa, the Yāma, and the Tuṣita heavens.

Of the Nirmāṇarati gods, the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods, the Brahmakāyika gods, the Brahmapurohita gods, the Brahmapārṣadya gods, the Mahābrahmans, the Parīttābha gods, the Apramāṇābha gods, the Ābhāsvara gods, the Parīttaśubha gods, the Apramāṇaśubha gods,
the Śubhakṛtsna gods, the Bṛhatphala gods, the Asaṃjñisattva gods, the Śuddhāvāsa gods, and the Sudṛśa gods.

The appearance in the world of the Sudarśanas, the Aspr̥has, the Atapas, the Akaniṣṭhas, and the gods who have reached the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—
this occurs for stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arhats, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas.
It is by depending upon the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva that the appearance of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksambuddhas occurs in the world;
it is by depending upon the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva that the appearance of the Three Jewels—namely, the Jewel of the Buddha, the Jewel of the Dharma, and the Jewel of the Saṅgha—occurs in the world;
and it is by depending upon the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva that all the worldly requisites for life appear.

Noble sons, there appears in the world the manifestation of food, drink, clothing, vehicles, beds, seats, and medicinal requisites for the sick; as well as the manifestation of gems, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, crystals, coral, gold, and silver; and even all the means of comfort—whether divine or human—that constitute the happiness of worldly existence and the happiness of nirvāṇa. All this, noble sons, [arises].

It is by relying on the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva that this occurs; for what reason? Because, sons of good family, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he enjoins beings to the six perfections: he causes them to give gifts, he enjoins them to ethical discipline, he establishes them in patience, he enjoins them to vigor, he establishes them in meditative concentration, and he enjoins them to wisdom.
By relying upon the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, sentient beings practice the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom;
practicing the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, they attain all mundane and supramundane prosperities.
Therefore, noble sons, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva exists for the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings.
He has entered upon the practice.

Then, at that time, the Blessed One extended his tongue-faculty from his mouth and covered this great trichiliocosm with it. Then, from that tongue-faculty, rays of light of many colors and various hues issued forth, illuminating world-systems in the eastern direction as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges. Thus...
In the southern, western, and northern directions, as well as in the direction below and above, they illuminated world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges.

Then, indeed, in the eastern direction, in world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, immeasurable and incalculable bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, having seen that array of light, questioned the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, in their respective buddha-fields: "Blessed One, whose power is this, by which such a radiance of light is seen?"

Those Buddhas, those Blessed Ones, spoke thus to those Bodhisattvas, those Mahāsattvas: "Noble sons, in the western direction, in the world-system called Sahā, there is a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Śākyamuni. He has extended his tongue-faculty from his mouth, and with a great radiance, [illuminates] world-systems in the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā."
Having thus clarified the teaching and the full manifestation of the *prajñāpāramitā* for the sake of the bodhisattvas,

the mahāsattvas, those bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas, spoke to those Tathāgatas as follows: "O Blessed One, we shall go to that Sahā world-system to see that Blessed One, Śākyamuni, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksambuddha."

In order to see, honor, and attend upon them, and to see those Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas assembled from the ten directions and to hear this Perfection of Wisdom, those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, said this:
"Sons of good family, if you now deem it the right time, [come] thus from the southern direction, the western, the northern, the intermediate directions, and from below and above."

In the direction of world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, immeasurable and incalculable bodhisattva mahāsattvas, having seen that array of light, questioned the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, in their respective buddha-fields: "Blessed One, whose power is this, by which such a manifestation of light is seen? Those Buddhas [replied].

The Blessed Ones spoke thus to those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas: "Sons of good family, in the world-system called Sahā, in the direction below, there is a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksambuddha named Śākyamuni. Having extended his tongue-faculty, he has illuminated world-systems in the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges with a great radiance, namely for the sake of the bodhisattvas."
In order to teach and fully illuminate the perfection of wisdom for the sake of the great beings,

those bodhisattva mahāsattvas spoke thus to those Tathāgatas: "O Blessed One, we shall go to that Sahā world-system to behold, pay homage to, and attend upon that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksambuddha Śākyamuni."

And to those Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who had gathered from the ten directions in order to see them, to pay homage, and to hear this Perfection of Wisdom, those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, said: "Noble sons, do you now consider it the right time?"
Then, indeed, those bodhisattvas from the ten directions, having taken hold of flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, and flags,
and having taken baskets of various jewels, gold, and silver flowers, approached the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, accompanied by a great concert of musical instruments, cymbals, and singing.

Then indeed, the gods of the Four Great Kings up to the Akaniṣṭha gods, taking divine flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, blue lotuses, red lotuses, white lotuses, night-blooming water lilies, white lotuses, maṇḍārava flowers, filaments, and tamāla leaves, approached the place where the Blessed One was. Then those bodhisattva mahāsattvas and those gods scattered those flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, and ointments over the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksambuddha.

Then indeed, those flowers, having risen into the air, were established above this great trichiliocosm as a flower-canopy— quadrangular, with four pillars, symmetrically divided, well-proportioned, delightful, and pleasing to the mind; and upon seeing that flower-canopy, the assembly of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas and the assembly of gods [were moved].

And by hundreds of thousands of myriads of kotis of living beings, the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) was attained; they rose from their seats, draped their upper robes over one shoulder, placed their right knees upon the ground, and extending their joined palms toward the Blessed One, addressed the Blessed One as follows: "O Blessed One, in the future..."

"May we become possessors of such qualities as these, just like the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksambuddha; and may we maintain a community of disciples and teach the Dharma in an assembly just as the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma now."

Then the Blessed One, having understood the disposition of those bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas who had arrived from the ten directions, as well as of those gods, and having recognized their receptivity to the non-arising, non-cessation, non-conditioning, and non-manifestation of all phenomena, smiled.

Then the venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, and extending his joined palms toward the Blessed One, addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"What, O Blessed One, is the cause, what is the condition for the manifestation of this smile? For Buddhas do not manifest a smile without cause or without condition."
When this was said, the Blessed One manifested a smile and addressed the venerable Ānanda:
"Ānanda, by means of these hundreds of thousands of nayutas of koṭis of living beings, the patient acceptance of non-arising phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) has been attained;
and in a future time, after sixty-eight billion eons, they shall become Tathāgatas, Arhats, named Bodhyaṅgapuṣpa."
Perfectly awakened Buddhas will arise in the world during the Puṣpākara eon.

Then, at that time, the Blessed One addressed the venerable Subhūti: "May it be inspired in you, Subhūti, to deliver a discourse concerning the perfection of wisdom of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas, so that bodhisattva mahāsattvas, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, may go forth [to liberation]."
Then, indeed, this thought occurred to those bodhisattvas mahāsattvas, those great śrāvakas, and those sons of gods:

"Will the venerable Subhūti indeed teach the perfection of wisdom to the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas, by means of the power of his own wisdom and eloquence, or rather through the majesty of the Buddha? Then the venerable Subhūti, having known with his own mind the reflection in the minds of those bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas, those great śrāvakas, and those sons of gods, [addressed] the venerable...

He said this to Śāriputra: "Venerable Śāriputra, whatever the disciples of the Blessed One speak, teach, or proclaim, all that should be understood as the personal agency of the Tathāgata. For what reason?
Because when the disciples of the Blessed One train in the teaching of the Dharma that has been taught by the Tathāgata, [it is his power]."

They realize the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā); having realized the true nature of phenomena, whatever they speak, teach, or instruct, all of that is not in contradiction with the true nature of phenomena. Śāriputra, it is the Tathāgata himself who, through the application of skillful means, will instruct the bodhisattva mahāsattvas in the perfection of wisdom; this is beyond the scope of the venerable Śāriputra.
[He taught] the instruction on the perfection of wisdom for all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas mahāsattvas.

Then the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, when it is said ‘bodhisattva, mahāsattva,’ of what dharma, Blessed One, is this a designation—namely, ‘bodhisattva’ or ‘perfection of wisdom’?
For I do not perceive that dharma, Blessed One.”
That is to say, "Bodhisattva" or "Perfection of Wisdom. Yet, O Blessed One,
since I do not perceive a Bodhisattva and do not apprehend a Perfection of Wisdom, which Bodhisattva shall I instruct and admonish, and in which Perfection of Wisdom?

When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti: "Subhūti, this is a mere name, namely 'perfection of wisdom' and 'bodhisattva,' and even that name is not apprehended internally, nor externally, nor in between the two. It is just as, Subhūti, when a being is designated by the name 'being.'"

And there is never any perception of a sentient being; that which is called a "sentient being" is merely a designation for phenomena (*dharmaprajñaptimātra*). And this designation of phenomena has neither arising nor cessation, except that it is conventionally expressed by means of mere names and symbols. Furthermore, that name is not perceived internally, nor externally, nor in between the two. In the same way, [the designations] self, sentient being, living soul, creature, nourisher, person, individual, human, man, agent, experiencer, progenitor, and seer are likewise [mere designations].

Thus, Subhūti, all this is merely a designation of phenomena (*dharmaprajñaptimātra*). And of that designation of phenomena there is neither arising nor cessation; it is only by means of mere names and conventions that it is expressed in worldly discourse. Furthermore, that name is not apprehended internally, nor externally, nor in between the two. In the very same way, Subhūti, that which is called "perfection of wisdom" (*prajñāpāramitā*) is [merely a designation] for a bodhisattva.

Thus, "Bodhisattva" by name—all this is merely a designation of phenomena (*dharmaprajñaptimātra*). And of that designation of phenomena, there is neither arising nor cessation; it is only by way of mere names and conventions that it is expressed in common usage. Furthermore, that name is not found internally, nor externally, nor in between the two. Subhūti, it is just as with this internal [designation].

"Form"—all this is merely a designation of phenomena (*dharmaprajñaptimātra*). And of that designation of phenomena there is neither arising nor cessation; it is only by means of mere names and conventions that it is expressed in worldly discourse. Furthermore, that name is not apprehended internally, nor externally, nor in between the two. In the same way, Subhūti, "feeling," "perception," "formative factors," and "consciousness" are merely designations of phenomena.

And for this designation of phenomena (*dharmaprajñapti*), there is neither arising nor cessation; it is expressed by means of mere names and conventions (*nāmasaṃketamātra*). Furthermore, that name is not apprehended internally, nor externally, nor in between the two. In the same way, Subhūti, that which is called "perfection of wisdom," "bodhisattva," or "the name of a bodhisattva"—all of this is merely a designation of phenomena.

And for that designation of phenomena (*dharmaprajñapti*), there is neither arising nor cessation; it is expressed by nothing other than mere name and convention. Furthermore, that name is not apprehended internally, nor externally, nor in between the two. Subhūti, "the eye" is merely a designation of phenomena; and for that designation of phenomena, there is neither arising nor cessation, except [as a conventional expression].
It is designated by means of a mere name and convention, yet that name is not found internally, nor externally, nor in between the two.

In the same way, Subhūti, the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are merely designations for phenomena (*dharmaprajñaptimātra*). Of that designation for phenomena, there is neither arising nor cessation; it is only by means of a mere conventional designation for phenomena that it is expressed in common usage. And that name is not apprehended internally, nor externally, nor in between the two. Thus, Subhūti, it is with regard to form... [and so on for the other aggregates].
This is merely a designation of phenomena (*dharmaprajñapti-mātra*). Of that designation of phenomena, there is neither arising nor cessation;
it is expressed by means of mere names and conventions. And that name is not apprehended internally, nor externally, nor in between the two.
In the same way, Subhūti, [it applies to] sound, odor, taste, tangible objects, and mental phenomena (*dharma*); such is the designation of phenomena.
